blocks.content: A container with no explicit USER instruction runs as root by default, and that default is one of the most common, and most fixable, security weaknesses in real-world Dockerfiles.

As covered briefly in the Dockerfile module, a container with no USER instruction runs its main process as root, UID 0, not because anyone deliberately decided that was a good idea, simply because it is what happens when nothing else is specified.

blocks.alt: root by default, unless something says otherwise

blocks.content: 2. What root Inside a Container Can Actually Do
blocks.text: 2. What root Inside a Container Can Actually Do

blocks.content: Within the container's own filesystem, a root process has no restrictions at all: it can read, write, or delete anything, install or remove packages, modify anything the application itself would never normally need to touch.

blocks.alt: Total control over everything inside the container

blocks.content: 3. Container root Is Usually Namespaced, But Not a Free Pass
blocks.text: 3. Container root Is Usually Namespaced, But Not a Free Pass

blocks.content: It is worth being precise: container UID 0 is, by default, mapped through Linux user namespaces and is not automatically identical to the host machine's real root account. That said, this is a meaningful but not absolute boundary, it significantly narrows, but does not eliminate, what a compromised root process inside a container could potentially do.

blocks.alt: A real but not absolute boundary between container root and host root

blocks.content: 4. Where the Real Escalation Risk Lives
blocks.text: 4. Where the Real Escalation Risk Lives

blocks.content: The boundary genuinely breaks down under specific misconfigurations: running a container with --privileged, or mounting the host's Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) into it, both hand a root process inside the container a real, practical path to affecting the host itself, not just the container.

blocks.alt: Specific misconfigurations turn container root into a real host risk

blocks.content: None of this means containers provide no isolation, they genuinely do. It means running as non-root is still a real, meaningful, low-cost safety margin, especially since it removes an entire class of "what if this specific process gets compromised" scenarios before they even become a question.

blocks.alt: A small, low-cost change with a real reduction in risk

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container with no USER instruction runs as root by default, with full control over everything inside its own filesystem.
Container root is usually namespaced away from real host root, but --privileged or a mounted docker.sock can turn it into genuine host-level risk.
